output.title: When a metric stops helping you decide
output.body:
If a metric no longer changes what you do, it has stopped being useful. That is the point where definitions start to matter less than the decision behind them.

A common small-business example is a metric that still gets reported, but no longer tells you whether to approve, reject, or pass a task back for review. The label stays the same while the workflow has moved on. Then the team keeps counting something that no one can act on.

That is usually a sign that one of two things happened: the work changed, or the rule changed. A new product, a new channel, or a new exception can make yesterday's metric too broad. Or the original rule may still be right, but the metric no longer captures it clearly.

The practical next step is simple: write down the real decision the metric is supposed to support, then check three recent cases where it failed. If you cannot tell from those cases whether the issue is the metric or the rule, the metric definition is not the problem you should fix first.

Once you know whether the metric or the rule broke, you'll know whether this is a reporting fix, a workflow redesign, or an automation opportunity.
